name: C#
year_note: Designed from January 1999 under the name COOL; announced at Microsoft's Professional Developers Conference in July 2000; C# 1.0 shipped with .NET Framework 1.0 in early 2002.
tagline: Microsoft's managed C-family language for .NET, which carried LINQ and async/await into the mainstream.
summary: C# is a statically typed, multi-paradigm language designed at Microsoft for the .NET platform, combining a Java-like managed object model with C++-style features, reified generics and a unified type system. It has absorbed functional and asynchronous ideas early, including LINQ, lambdas, async/await, pattern matching and records, and carried several of them into the mainstream. Open source and cross-platform since .NET Core, it is used for web services, desktop and mobile apps, and games built with the Unity engine.
history:
In January 1999 Anders Hejlsberg, previously involved in the design of Turbo Pascal, Delphi and Visual J++, formed a Microsoft team to build a new language for the .NET Framework, initially called COOL ('C-like Object Oriented Language'). Renamed C#, it was announced at the Professional Developers Conference in July 2000, standardized as ECMA-334 in December 2001 (ISO/IEC 23270 in 2003), and shipped as C# 1.0 with .NET Framework 1.0 in 2002. James Gosling and Bill Joy called it an imitation of Java; Hejlsberg replied that it was 'not a Java clone' and 'much closer to C++' in its design.

Later versions added generics reified in the runtime, iterators and anonymous methods (2.0, 2005), LINQ with lambdas and local type inference (3.0, 2007), dynamic binding (4.0, 2010) and async/await (5.0, 2012), a model JavaScript, Python, Rust and Swift later adopted. In 2014 Microsoft open-sourced the Roslyn compiler and announced the cross-platform .NET Core, which became the main line of .NET with .NET 5 (2020).

Since C# 7.0 (2017) the language has gained tuples, pattern matching, nullable reference types, records and less ceremony, such as top-level statements (C# 9) and, with .NET 10 and C# 14 (2025), single-file programs run with `dotnet run app.cs`.
innovations: LINQ: language-integrated queries over collections, databases and XML, built on lambdas, extension methods and expression trees
async/await keywords (C# 5, 2012), the model later adopted by JavaScript, Python, Rust and Swift
Generics reified in the runtime (C# 2.0), unlike Java's type erasure
Properties, events and delegates as language features for component-oriented programming
A unified type system in which value types (structs) and reference types share System.Object as their root

typing.notes: `var` infers local variable types (C# 3.0); `dynamic` (C# 4.0) opts individual expressions into run-time binding; nullable reference types (C# 8.0) add flow-analysed null warnings.

influenced_by.note: Managed, garbage-collected, single-inheritance object model with interfaces, compiled to bytecode for a VM.
Syntax plus structs, operator overloading, enums and unsafe pointers.
C-family statement and expression syntax, largely via C++.
LINQ's query comprehensions and lambdas drew on functional programming research (via Cω).
Type inference, tuples and pattern matching in later versions.
yield-based iterators (C# 2.0) descend from CLU's iterators.

Hejlsberg's Delphi: native properties ('Delphi was the first product I worked on to natively support properties, and then that got carried over to C#'), events, and bound method pointers that became delegates (via Visual J++), within a component-oriented design.
Properties and events for rapid application development.

influenced_by_external.name: Visual J++
influenced_by_external.note: Microsoft's Java implementation, which Hejlsberg worked on; delegates first appeared there.

influenced_by_external.name: Cω
influenced_by_external.note: Microsoft Research language whose query and stream features led to LINQ.

exceptions.note: try/catch/finally and exception filters (`when`); exceptions are unchecked.

generators.note: `yield return` iterators; async iterators (IAsyncEnumerable) since C# 8.0.

pattern-matching.note: Extended through switch expressions and positional/property patterns (8.0), relational and logical patterns (9.0) and list patterns (11).

type-inference.note: `var`, lambda parameter and generic method inference; target-typed `new()` (C# 9).

generics.note: Reified by the CLR, so List<int> stores unboxed ints; constraints with `where`.

algebraic-data-types.note: Records and positional deconstruction give product types; sum types are emulated with abstract records, as the language has no closed unions.

type-classes.note: Static abstract interface members enable type-class-style generic math (INumber<T>), though types opt in at their declaration.

option-types.note: Nullable reference types (T?) give compile-time null warnings; Nullable<T> covers value types since C# 2.0.

gradual-typing.note: The `dynamic` type defers member lookup to run time inside statically typed code.

interfaces.note: Default interface methods since C# 8.0 and static abstract members since C# 11.

inheritance.note: Single class inheritance, multiple interface implementation.

everything-is-an-object.note: Unified type system: every type, including int, derives from System.Object (value types via boxing), but computation is not message passing.

traits-mixins.note: Default interface methods; extension methods (C# 3.0) and extension members (C# 14) add methods to existing types.

modules.note: Namespaces plus assemblies as units of separate compilation and deployment, with `internal` visibility.

first-class-functions.note: Delegates since 1.0, anonymous methods in 2.0 and lambdas in 3.0 (2007).

closures.note: Anonymous methods and lambdas capture variables by reference.

immutability.note: readonly fields and structs, init-only setters and records (C# 9), but mutability is the default.

list-comprehensions.note: LINQ query expressions (from ... where ... select) are comprehension syntax that compiles to method calls.

lazy-evaluation.note: LINQ operators and iterators use deferred execution; Lazy<T> for lazy values.

pointers.note: Pointers and pointer arithmetic are allowed in `unsafe` code; Span<T> and ref structs cover most low-level needs safely.

csp-channels.note: System.Threading.Channels in the standard library (.NET Core 3.0).

async-await.note: Modelled on F# asynchronous workflows; the compiler rewrites async methods into state machines.

reflection.note: System.Reflection, custom attributes and expression trees.

compile-time-execution.note: Roslyn source generators run user code inside the compiler to generate source; there is no general constexpr.

hot-code-reload.note: Edit and Continue and .NET Hot Reload apply code edits to a running process.

declarative-queries.note: LINQ queries can be translated from expression trees into SQL by providers such as Entity Framework.

milestones.event: C# 1.0 ships with .NET Framework 1.0 and Visual Studio .NET
C# 2.0: generics, iterators, anonymous methods, nullable value types
C# 3.0: LINQ, lambdas, var, extension methods
C# 4.0: dynamic binding, named and optional arguments
C# 8.0: nullable reference types, switch expressions, default interface methods
C# 14 and .NET 10: extension members, file-based `dotnet run app.cs`

trivia: The name comes from musical notation, where a sharp raises a note by a semitone; the # also resembles four + signs arranged in a grid, echoing C++.
The team's working name for the language was COOL, for 'C-like Object Oriented Language', dropped for trademark reasons.

hello.notes: Top-level statements (C# 9) remove the class/Main boilerplate, and .NET 10 runs a single .cs file without a project file. The classic form is `class Program { static void Main() { ... } }`.

factorial.code:
Console.WriteLine(Factorial(10));

static long Factorial(int n) => n <= 1 ? 1 : n * Factorial(n - 1);
factorial.notes: A static local function declared after the top-level statements, with an expression body (=>).

fizzbuzz.notes: A switch expression over a tuple, using discards (_) as wildcards (C# 8).

higher-order.notes: Query syntax compiles to method calls: Enumerable.Range(1, 10).Where(n => n % 2 == 0).Select(n => n * n). Evaluation is deferred until string.Join enumerates the result.

shapes.notes: Records (C# 9) with positional patterns in a switch expression. Record hierarchies are open to extension, so the switch needs a fallback arm to be exhaustive. [...] is a collection expression (C# 12).

signature.title: async/await
signature.expected_output:
slow: started
fast: started
fast: done
slow: done
total = 42
signature.notes: Both calls start immediately and run concurrently; `await` suspends without blocking a thread, and top-level code may await directly. The output order depends on the two delays (50 ms and 300 ms).

toolchains.name: .NET SDK (file-based apps)
toolchains.install: Self-built image: FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0; ENV DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=1 DOTNET_NOLOGO=1 NuGetAudit=false; RUN one warm-up `dotnet run warm.cs` so the NuGet cache is populated for offline restores
toolchains.notes: The plain mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 image fails under --network none because the implicit restore tries to reach nuget.org. {file} must end in .cs. Also verified with the host .NET SDK 10.0.112.

browser.name: Roslyn on Blazor WebAssembly (C# minor)
browser.notes: The Roslyn compiler and .NET runtime running as WebAssembly compile and run C# client-side; a large initial download.

runtime.notes: After warm-up, each file compiles and runs in well under a second.
